summary: Jon Postel's comment on RFC 467, endorsing its proposal to resynchronize the state of a Host-Host connection with one small change. He suggests naming the commands RAS and RAR, reset allocation sender and receiver, since only the allocation is reset, and includes a table of the procedure.

plainLanguage.summary: This RFC comments on a proposed way to resynchronize a host-to-host connection. Postel endorses the procedure and suggests names that clarify that it resets allocation, not the whole connection.

subtitle: Jon Postel's naming change for a connection-allocation recovery procedure.

tldr.problem: RFC 467 proposed a procedure for resynchronizing connection status between a sender and receiver.
tldr.mechanism: Postel endorses the procedure and proposes the names RAS and RAR because only allocation is reset.
tldr.outcome: The RFC gives a concise interpretation of the proposed sender and receiver steps, without replacing RFC 467.

sections.title: A Comment on Connection Resynchronization
sections.content: Jon Postel comments on the resynchronization procedure proposed by Burchfiel and Tomlinson in RFC 467. He endorses their proposal with a naming change and says his condensed table is meant to clarify, not supersede, their document.
sections.plainLanguage: Postel supports the procedure in RFC 467. He proposes clearer command names and provides a shorter explanation of the sequence.

sections.title: The RAS and RAR Names
sections.content: Postel proposes the names RAS, for reset connection allocation sender, and RAR, for reset connection allocation receiver. He says these names are more appropriate because the procedure resets allocation, which is one aspect of a connection.
sections.plainLanguage: RAS and RAR name the sender and receiver steps. The names emphasize that allocation is reset, not the entire connection.

sections.title: Sender and Receiver Steps
sections.content:
The table shows the sender waiting until no RFNM is outstanding, sending RAS, and processing allocates until RAR arrives. The receiver sends RAR, processes messages until RAS arrives, zeros allocation quantities, returns to open state, and sends a new allocate.

Either side can initiate the procedure for internal reasons or after receiving RAS or RAR, as the RFC explains.
sections.plainLanguage: The sender and receiver exchange RAS and RAR, reset their allocation quantities, and return to the open state. Either side may start the procedure.

references.text: Burchfiel, J. and Tomlinson, R., "Proposed Host-Host Protocol", RFC 467, 1973.
